title: Weather elasticity of Citi Bike trips by hour-of-week and rider type: 2023 fit, 2024 replication
description: If member/casual labels reflect trip purpose, then weather sensitivity should follow purpose within each rider type. H1: member weekday commute-window cells (7-9h and 17-19h) have the smallest temperature elasticity above about 10C and the smallest rain penalty among all cells. H2: casual riders and weekend-midday cells have the largest temperature and rain elasticities. H3: the member-casual elasticity gap shrinks inside weekday commute windows, which would indicate that purpose and not membership drives sensitivity. The pre-stated replication criterion is that the rank ordering of cells by elasticity fitted on 2023 is reproduced in 2024 (Spearman rho of cell elasticities above 0.7, with the sign of the commute-versus-leisure contrast preserved). Results are described as associations, not causal effects.
research_questions: Descriptive Citi Bike patterns are well documented. Existing weather work is mostly daily (e.g., Schneider) or hourly but focused on bike type (36.2M trips, 2023); neither resolves hour of day by rider type (literature recalled from a brief search, unverified). The claim that members commute and casual riders are leisure users is inferred from demand shapes and rarely tested under weather stress. Gap: does weather sensitivity across hour-of-week cells and rider types match what those labels predict?
proposed_methods: Data: Citi Bike monthly trip files, 2023 and 2024 (s3.amazonaws.com/tripdata; if download fails, stop and report). Verify schema (rider type, bike type, timestamp formats) rather than assuming. Cleaning waterfall with counts per rule: missing timestamps, non-positive durations, under 60 s with same start/end station, over 24 h, duplicate ride IDs, out-of-year starts. Aggregate to hourly counts by rider type x bike type; add daily/monthly summaries for Q1-Q3 with week-block bootstrap CIs. Weather: hourly temperature, precipitation, wind from NOAA or Open-Meteo (Central Park primary; second site as sensitivity if easy). Model: negative-binomial (or quasi-Poisson) GLM per cell (rider type x weekday/weekend x hour, optionally x bike type) with spline in temperature, wet-hour indicator, rain intensity, wind, and week-of-year fixed effects so identification is within-week. Sensitivity: smooth day-of-year plus 24 h lagged weather instead; pooled model with hour x temperature interactions; rain lags (0, 1, 3 h); apparent temperature. Flag holidays and extreme-event days (e.g., September 2023 flooding, heat, snow); show results with and without. Summaries per cell: effect of +10C from 10-20C and 20-30C; percent change for 1 mm/h rain vs dry. Inference: week-block bootstrap (at least 1000 resamples) for elasticities and contrasts (commute vs midday, member vs casual). Replication: fit on 2023, compare 2024 cell elasticities, predict 2024 hourly counts with calibration by weather bin. Save code, tables, figures and a short report (3-5 findings; limitations: single city, single-station weather attenuation, member/casual definition changes, bike-mix shift, non-causal framing).
expected_outcomes: A cleaning waterfall table with counts removed per rule for both years.
Descriptive figures and tables for Q1-Q3 (monthly volume with peak/trough, day-of-week x hour heatmaps, member vs casual profiles) with week-block bootstrap CIs and a 2023 vs 2024 comparison.
A heatmap of temperature elasticity and rain penalty by hour-of-week cell and rider type with bootstrap CIs, showing whether commute-hour member cells are the least weather-sensitive.
A replication table: 2023-fitted vs 2024 cell elasticities, rank correlation, and out-of-sample calibration of predicted 2024 hourly counts.
A robustness table covering seasonal control choice, rain lag windows, bike-type stratification, extreme-day exclusion and weather station choice.
A short report with 3 to 5 findings, each with a figure or table, plus stated limitations and a non-causal framing.
hypothesis: If member/casual labels reflect trip purpose, then weather sensitivity should follow purpose within each rider type. H1: member weekday commute-window cells (7-9h and 17-19h) have the smallest temperature elasticity above about 10C and the smallest rain penalty among all cells. H2: casual riders and weekend-midday cells have the largest temperature and rain elasticities. H3: the member-casual elasticity gap shrinks inside weekday commute windows, which would indicate that purpose and not membership drives sensitivity. The pre-stated replication criterion is that the rank ordering of cells by elasticity fitted on 2023 is reproduced in 2024 (Spearman rho of cell elasticities above 0.7, with the sign of the commute-versus-leisure contrast preserved). Results are described as associations, not causal effects.
alternatives_considered: (1) A pure 2023 vs 2024 descriptive replication with bootstrap CIs: this was the rejected proposal and is retained only as the Q1-Q3 baseline layer, not the headline. (2) Station-level commuter vs leisure clustering with Gaussian mixtures: richer spatially but already published and needs station metadata handling; it also lacks a sharp falsifiable prediction. (3) Daily-resolution weather regression as in prior work: simpler, but cannot separate hour-of-day effects from the diurnal temperature cycle and cannot test the purpose hypothesis by hour. (4) Pooled hourly model with hour x temperature interactions instead of per-cell fits: more efficient and less noisy, kept as a robustness check against per-cell overfitting.
falsification_check: Refuted if: (a) after bike-type stratification and week fixed effects, bootstrap CIs for commute-vs-midday and member-vs-casual elasticity contrasts include zero; (b) the 2023 cell ordering fails in 2024 (Spearman rho under 0.7 or contrast sign flips); (c) the commute-window member advantage vanishes under the alternative seasonal control or when extreme days are excluded; (d) the member-casual gap does not shrink in commute windows (H3 fails). Finding that labels do not predict weather behaviour is itself a reportable result.
unresolved_disagreements: Whether week-of-year fixed effects suffice to separate weather from seasonal confounding, or whether a smooth day-of-year term plus lagged weather should be the primary specification.
Whether hourly precipitation from a single Central Park station is defensible, or whether averaging two or three stations is needed; the bias from spatial mismatch is unquantified.
Whether per-cell fits or a pooled model with interactions is the better primary specification given multiple-comparison and noise concerns.
Whether the novelty gap (hour-resolved, rider-type-resolved weather response on Citi Bike) really exists; my literature search was brief and an unseen paper could cover it.

decision.rationale:
I chose Idea B. It is the only proposal that turns the briefing's descriptive questions into a genuinely open, falsifiable one: do the standard 'member = commuter, casual = leisure' labels — which the literature infers from the shape of demand profiles — actually predict behavior under weather stress, hour by hour? That is new knowledge rather than re-verification: B cites the closest prior work (a 2023 hourly panel study) and shows it covers bike type, not rider type by hour, and it names a specific unhandled confound (ordinary diurnal temperature covariation) that naive hourly models would trip on. The design is the strongest of the three on guards against misleading results: week-of-year fixed effects so identification comes from within-week weather variation, a temperature spline, stratification by bike type to avoid mix-shift artifacts, holiday handling, week-block bootstrap, out-of-sample replication of the elasticity ordering from 2023 to 2024, and explicit refutation criteria including an informative null. It avoids circularity by testing profile-derived purpose labels on an independent dimension (weather response). Feasibility is confirmed by the screening (S3 reachable, weather APIs reachable, aggregation to a small panel is cheap), and it still delivers the Q1–Q3 baseline as a layer under the headline, so the required short report is not at risk. Its weaknesses — novelty based on a brief literature search, single-station weather attenuation, hourly rain misalignment — are acknowledged and have planned sensitivity checks.

Idea A was not chosen. Its hook — that e-bikes flatten seasonality and weather response — is substantially anticipated by work the group itself surfaced (the 2023 hourly panel finding that e-bikes buffer temperature losses), and A's own supporting evidence is journalistic (a Cycling Weekly anecdote, a fleet-share news item), so the new-knowledge increment is thin. More damaging, A has an unresolved confound it raises but does not fix: e-bike fleet share grew rapidly within 2023–2024 and e-bike trips are supply- and availability-constrained, so stratified seasonal ratios would mix rider behavior with fleet expansion and docking/charging availability, neither of which is measurable in the trip files. Its refutation framing is also underdetermined — a proportional winter drop cannot cleanly separate 'exposure/safety' from 'exertion' with this data.

Idea C was not chosen. It is the most feasible and the most honest about causality, and its denominator control is a genuinely useful robustness layer — but the deliverable is an accounting decomposition (continuing vs entrant vs exit stations) that mostly de-risks the standard descriptive report rather than answering an open question about usage patterns; by its own framing, a null result 'validates the simpler aggregate report,' which is groundwork, not new knowledge. Its one behavioral hypothesis (entrant stations skew member/weekday/commute) is speculative and, if confirmed, describes where expansion went rather than how people ride; and the entrant/continuing classification rests on fragile station identity (ID changes, an 'observed station-day' proxy for open status), so measurement error could drive the headline. Relative to the screening's objection that the previous proposal was 'a modest increment over a descriptive replication, not an open question,' C stays closer to that territory than B.

contributions.content:
I agree with the reviewer's feedback on the previous proposal: replicating the summer peak and the bimodal weekday commute is too vanilla, even with rigorous bootstrapped confidence intervals. We need a hook that makes these exact same descriptive questions interesting. 

Here is my proposal for how we can pivot.

**1. The Gap**
The briefing asks us to analyze usage over time (monthly, daily, hourly), by user type, and optionally by weather. The gap in the previous proposal was treating all bikes as a monolith. The system has fundamentally changed in the last few years, and the real question isn't "what is the seasonality of bike share?", but rather "how does the massive shift to e-bikes alter the established laws of bike-share physics?"

**2. Prior Work**
- The baseline temporal patterns (summer peak, weekday bimodal commute, weekend midday peak) are thoroughly documented (e.g., O'Mahony & Shmoys; numerous recent MDPI papers). 
- However, e-bikes have radically reshaped the system. A September 2026 piece from *Micromobility.io* notes that e-bikes recently grew to nearly 50% of the Citi Bike fleet and now account for over 70% of all rides.
- There is anecdotal evidence that e-bikes change behavioral friction. A 2022 *Cycling Weekly* article claimed that while overall Citi Bike ridership drops 60% from October to February, e-bike usage "held firm," suggesting that quicker journey times and less physical exertion make winter commuting more viable. 

**3. Main Research Idea: E-bikes as a friction isolator**
- **Question:** Does electric assistance insulate bike-share usage from traditional friction factors like seasonality, weather, and the physical exertion of commuting?
- **Hypothesis:** E-bikes will exhibit significantly "flatter" seasonality and weather-response curves than classic bikes, and sharper weekday commute peaks, because motor assistance overcomes the sweat/exertion penalty of riding to work or riding in the cold. 
- **Method:** We answer all the briefing's required questions, but we stratify every single plot and summary stat by `rideable_type` (classic vs. electric) using 2023 and 2024 data. 
  - *Monthly:* Calculate the seasonal peak-to-trough volume ratio separately for e-bikes and classic bikes.
  - *Day/Hour:* Compare the weekday commute peak-to-base ratio for both types.
  - *User type:* Cross-tabulate `member_casual` with `rideable_type` to see if members preferentially eat the e-bike per-minute surcharges to commute.
  - *Weather (Optional):* Regress daily trip counts on temperature/precipitation separately for classic and e-bikes to compare their weather-penalty coefficients.
- **Refutation:** If e-bike volume drops proportionally just as much as classic bikes in winter or rain, it tells us that weather seasonality is strictly about exposure/safety (ice, cold wind), not physical exertion.
- **Why it matters:** It upgrades a standard descriptive report into a strategic insight about urban mobility. If e-bikes are weather-resistant, electrifying the fleet is the key to year-round financial sustainability for bike-share systems.
- **Feasibility:** Fully feasible in the container. `rideable_type` is a standard, well-populated column in the 2023/2024 monthly CSVs. The computational cost is identical to the rejected proposal.

**4. Alternatives Considered**
- *Spatial/OD Network analysis:* Looking at how destination patterns have shifted. I prefer the e-bike stratification because the briefing explicitly asks for temporal usage patterns (monthly, daily, hourly), and spatial analysis adds mapping complexity that might break the "short report" constraint.
- *Post-COVID vs Pre-COVID comparison:* Comparing 2019 to 2024. I rejected this because the data schemas changed significantly (e.g., `rideable_type` wasn't consistently tracked before 2021, and station ID formats changed), which introduces unnecessary data-cleaning risk.

Does anyone see a flaw in relying on the `rideable_type` field for this, or have thoughts on how to handle the fact that the overall fleet size of e-bikes was growing during this period?

contributions.content:
## 1. The question and where the gap is

The briefing asks for a descriptive report on seasonality, day-of-week and hour-of-day patterns, and member vs casual differences, with an optional weather association. The screening feedback says the headline patterns are already well documented, and I agree. A replication with a bootstrap would only be a modest increment.

I think the gap is the weather question, and the optional Q4 is the right place to look for new content. Existing Citi Bike weather work is almost all at **daily** resolution:
- Schneider found trips ramp up quickly between 30 and 60°F, with a much weaker relationship above about 60°F. This used daily Central Park data.
- A climate-impact study found ridden hours and distance rose with temperature, then declined above 26–28°C.
- A recent GitHub forecasting write-up reports that 10→20°C raises trips +24% for members and +62% for casual riders, and 10 mm of rain lowers them −28% and −38%. I have not verified that analysis, and it is a daily model.
- A 2023 hourly panel study of 36.2M trips finds temperature-induced losses are 5.6 and 7.7 percentage points smaller for e-bikes than for classic bikes. It is about bike type, not time of day or rider type.

Two things look under-examined, though I only searched briefly:
- **Hour-resolved weather sensitivity.** How does weather sensitivity vary across the hour-of-week profile, split by rider type?
- **Ordinary diurnal temperature covariation.** Temperature rises through the day. Naive hourly models can therefore confuse hour-of-day effects with temperature effects.

On the rider-type literature, the standard story is that subscribers use bikeshare more for work trips and casual users more for leisure. That story is usually inferred from the shape of the demand profile. It is rarely tested through behaviour under stress, such as weather.

## 2. What prior work has established

- **Seasonality and commute peaks:** well established. Citi Bike is commuter-like for members and leisure-like for casual riders (sources above, plus the TRID/ScienceDirect member vs casual study: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2214367X24000565).
- **The pandemic shifted the profile:** one report says weekday rides used to outnumber weekend rides by about 10%, then weekend rides exceeded weekday rides. That report is about DC (CaBi), not NYC. A NYC study finds the pandemic reduced member weekday trips. So 2023–24 is a post-pandemic "new normal" and I would not assume pre-2020 shapes.
- **Weather is nonlinear and rain-sensitive** (sources above).

## 3. Main idea: the weather-sensitivity profile as a purpose test

**Question.** Do the standard "member = commuter, casual = leisure" labels predict how trips respond to weather, hour by hour? If the labels reflect trip purpose, commute-hour member trips should be less weather-elastic than weekend-midday trips.

**Hypotheses.** Let ε(h, daytype, rider) be the log-rate response to temperature and to rain, estimated per hour-of-week cell.
- **H1.** Member weekday 7–9 and 17–19h trips have the smallest temperature elasticity above about 10°C, and the smallest rain penalty relative to leisure cells.
- **H2.** Casual and weekend-midday cells have the largest elasticities.
- **H3.** The rider-type gap in elasticity shrinks inside the commute windows. That would show purpose, not membership, drives sensitivity.

**Method.**
- **Data:** 2023 and 2024 Citi Bike trips, aggregated to counts per hour × rider type × bike type. Use hourly weather from NOAA or Open-Meteo for Central Park/NYC. Screening confirmed the container has outbound internet and S3 is reachable.
- **Model:** Poisson or negative-binomial GLM per (rider type, daytype, hour-of-day) cell. Use a spline for temperature, rain as intensity or a wet indicator, and wind. Control with week-of-year fixed effects so identification comes from within-week weather variation rather than from seasonal trend. Holidays are flagged and excluded or modeled separately.
- **Uncertainty:** block bootstrap by week.
- **Replication:** fit on 2023, then predict 2024 profiles out of sample. Report whether the ordering of cells by elasticity replicates.
- **Stratify by bike type** (classic vs e-bike), since e-bikes are known to buffer temperature effects. This avoids a mix-shift artifact.
- **Cleaning waterfall:** report counts removed for each rule.

**What would refute it.**
- Elasticity profiles are flat across hours and rider types after bike-type stratification.
- The ordering does not replicate from 2023 to 2024.
- The commute-hour member advantage disappears once week fixed effects and the bike-type split are applied.

Either outcome is informative. Finding the labels do not predict weather behaviour would be a real result.

**Why it matters.** It converts the descriptive hour-of-day and member vs casual profiles (Q2, Q3) into a test of what those profiles mean, using Q4. It also yields a practical output: which hours' demand is robust to weather, which matters for rebalancing. It stays non-causal, as the briefing requires. Weather exposure is plausibly exogenous within a week, but I would still call the results associations.

**Feasibility.** This is aggregation over about 100M rows into a small panel. That is a few thousand rows per cell, so modelling is cheap. Risks:
- **Single-point weather proxy.** Central Park is one station for the whole city. This attenuates the estimates, so I would say so.
- **Schema changes.** The rider-type field (member_casual) and the ride_id/bike-type schema differ across years. I'll verify this in the container rather than assume it.
- **Rain timing.** Hourly rain is noisy and misaligned with trip starts. A lag or window sensitivity check would show how much this matters.
- **Sampling error.** Counts are very large, so most uncertainty will come from weather-day sampling, not trips. The week-block bootstrap handles that.

## 4. Alternatives I considered

- **Station-level commuter vs leisure clustering (a GMM, as in the ScienceDirect paper above).** It is richer spatially but already done, and it needs station metadata handling. I prefer the weather-profile idea because it has a falsifiable prediction.
- **A pure 2023 vs 2024 replication with bootstrap CIs.** This is the rejected proposal. I would keep it as the baseline layer (Q1–Q3) because it supports the weather analysis, but not as the headline.

**Question for others:** is a week-of-year fixed effect enough to separate weather from seasonal confounding, or should we also include a smooth day-of-year term plus a lagged-weather control? I'd also like a view on whether hourly rain from a single station is defensible or whether we should average two or three stations.

contributions.content:
## 1. Question and real gap

The requested seasonal, weekday/weekend, and member/casual patterns are useful descriptive checks, but they are not themselves open questions. The literature already documents warm-season peaks, weekday commute peaks, weekend midday use, and stronger leisure signatures among casual riders.

The more consequential gap is **denominator control**: Citi Bike’s station network changes over time, so total trip growth can arise from:

1. more stations or station-days—the **extensive margin**;
2. more trips at continuing stations—the **intensive margin**; or
3. a shift toward different neighborhoods, rider types, and time periods.

A standard aggregate comparison can therefore mistake network expansion for changing rider behavior. The briefing’s screened proposal did not separate these mechanisms. The present analysis cannot estimate the causal effect of expansion, but it can provide an exact accounting of where observed growth occurred.

## 2. What prior work establishes

- Early NYC Citi Bike data show summer/autumn highs and winter lows. Subscribers exhibited morning and evening peaks, while customers had a midday peak and longer trips, consistent with—but not proving—commute versus leisure use. DOI: **10.1371/journal.pone.0232957**. ([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0232957&type=printable))
- Weather is already well studied. NYC ridership is strongly associated with weather, and temperature has a nonlinear relationship with use, declining above roughly 26–28°C in one study. DOIs: **10.1016/j.jtrangeo.2019.04.016** and **10.1289/EHP4039**. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0966692318307282?utm_source=openai))
- Station-level work has identified home-, work-, park-, and mixed-use temporal roles, as well as directional morning/evening imbalance. DOI: **10.1017/nws.2021.21**. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/network-science/article/role-detection-in-bicyclesharing-networks-using-multilayer-stochastic-block-models/5D73728650C5C3E2DB9455FCDF46F0E2))
- Expansion is known to alter both aggregate demand and use of incumbent stations; a longitudinal study in China found that new stations could attract use while also redistributing demand away from old stations. DOI: **10.1371/journal.pone.0168604**. ([openalex.org](https://openalex.org/W2563436444?utm_source=openai))
- NYC trip-generation research has modeled season, user type, and newly opened stations, but using much earlier system configurations. DOI: **10.1016/j.tra.2016.08.030**. ([ideas.repec.org](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/transa/v94y2016icp164-181.html?utm_source=openai))
- Citi Bike states that its published histories already omit staff/test-station trips and trips below 60 seconds. Our cleaning waterfall should distinguish these upstream filters from additional exclusions we impose. ([citibikenyc.com](https://citibikenyc.com/system-data?utm_source=openai))

Thus, the opportunity is not another demonstration of commute peaks. It is a **recent, exposure-aware decomposition of those peaks and annual growth in an expanding network**.

## 3. Main research idea: expansion-adjusted usage accounting

### Question

**How much of the difference in Citi Bike usage between 2023 and 2024 occurred at continuing stations versus stations entering or leaving the observed network, and did those margins have different member/casual and hourly signatures?**

### Hypothesis

The raw increase in trips will be materially larger than the increase within a matched cohort of continuing stations, and trips from newly observed stations will be disproportionately member, weekday, and commute-period trips. **(my claim, unverified)**

At the same time, the basic seasonal peak/trough and member-versus-casual temporal contrast should remain visible among matched continuing stations. **(my claim, unverified)**

### Data and cleaning

Use all 2023 and 2024 monthly trip files. The briefing’s screening found that the files are downloadable, storage is ample, and DuckDB or Polars can be installed.

Produce a cleaning waterfall for:

- missing or unparsable timestamps;
- end time not after start time;
- implausibly long trips, with **24 hours as the primary ceiling** and **4 hours as a sensitivity analysis**;
- missing rider type;
- missing start-station identity, excluded only from station-cohort analyses.

Because Citi Bike already filters sub-60-second trips, verify rather than silently applying that filter again. ([citibikenyc.com](https://citibikenyc.com/system-data?utm_source=openai))

### Concrete observables and comparisons

1. **Required baseline:** monthly trips, day-of-week/hour heatmaps, and separate member/casual profiles.

2. **Station cohorts by calendar month:**
   - continuing: observed as a start station in the same month of both years;
   - entrant: observed only in 2024;
   - exit: observed only in 2023.

   Use station ID as the primary key. As a robustness check, reconcile likely ID changes using normalized names and coordinates within a small tolerance.

3. **Exact accounting decomposition:**  
   For each calendar month and rider/time stratum, divide the 2024–2023 trip difference into:
   - change at matched continuing stations;
   - trips at 2024-only stations;
   - subtraction of trips at 2023-only stations.

   This is an accounting identity, **not a causal estimate of expansion’s effect**, because new stations may change demand at nearby incumbent stations.

4. **Exposure-adjusted intensity:**  
   Calculate trips per observed station-day for continuing and entrant cohorts. “Observed station-day” means at least one originating trip, since historical station-open status is not directly supplied; this limitation must be explicit.

5. **Composition tests:**  
   Compare cohorts on:
   - member share;
   - weekday share;
   - AM peak share, e.g. 07:00–10:00;
   - PM peak share, e.g. 16:00–20:00;
   - weekend midday share;
   - normalized 24-hour profiles.

6. **Uncertainty:**  
   Bootstrap days, not individual trips, to obtain intervals for monthly matched-station growth and differences in rider/time shares. Report effect sizes rather than relying primarily on p-values.

### Key figures

1. Raw monthly trips versus matched-continuing-station trips.
2. Monthly waterfall: continuing-station change, entrants, and exits.
3. Member/casual weekday-hour heatmaps for continuing versus entrant stations.
4. Table of cohort volume, trips per observed station-day, member share, and commute-period share.

### Refutation criteria

The hypothesis would be operationally refuted if:

- entrants and exits account for less than about 5% of the annual trip difference;
- raw and matched-station year-over-year growth differ by less than two percentage points across most months; and
- entrant stations’ member, weekday, and commute-period shares are indistinguishable from continuing stations within day-bootstrap intervals.

A null result would still be valuable: it would validate the simpler aggregate report despite network change.

### Why it matters

This distinguishes **system reach** from **use intensity** and indicates whether recent growth resembles extension of a commuter transport network or simply more use of the established core. It also makes the required seasonal report more defensible: readers can see whether its peaks are behavioral or partly compositional.

### Feasibility

High. The analysis needs only fields already present in the trip files and streaming group-bys; no weather or land-use join is required. It can be completed within the container and still deliver the requested short report, code, figures, cleaning counts, and limitations.

## 4. Alternatives considered
